# file_guard - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/file-guard/

## Expand description

A cross-platform library for simple advisory file locking.

The lock supports both exclusive and shared locking modes for a byte range
of an opened `File` object. Exclusively locking a portion of a file denies
all other processes both shared and exclusive access to the specified
region of the file. Shared locking a portion of a file denies all processes
exclusive access to the specified region of the file. The locked range does
not need to exist within the file, and the ranges may be used for any
arbitrary advisory locking protocol between processes.

The result of a [ lock()](https://docs.rs/fn.lock.html),

[, or](https://docs.rs/fn.try_lock.html)

`try_lock()`[is a](https://docs.rs/fn.lock_any.html)

`lock_any()`[. When dropped, this](https://docs.rs/struct.FileGuard.html)

`FileGuard`[will unlock the region of the file currently held. Exclusive locks may be](https://docs.rs/struct.FileGuard.html)

`FileGuard`[’ed to either a shared lock cross platform.](https://docs.rs/struct.FileGuard.html#method.downgrade)

`.downgrade()`On Unix systems `fcntl` is used to perform the locking, and on Windows, `LockFileEx`.
All generally available behavior is consistent across platforms. For platform-
specific behavior, traits may be used for the respective platform. For example,
on Windows, locks cannot be safely upgraded, whereas on Unix systems, this can
be done safely and atomically. To use this feature, the
[ file_guard::os::unix::FileGuardExt](https://docs.rs/os/unix/trait.FileGuardExt.html) may

`use`ed, enabling the [and](https://docs.rs/os/unix/trait.FileGuardExt.html#tymethod.upgrade)

`.upgrade()`[methods.](https://docs.rs/os/unix/trait.FileGuardExt.html#tymethod.try_upgrade)

`.try_upgrade()`Note that on Windows, the file must be open with write permissions to lock it.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use file_guard::Lock;
use std::fs::OpenOptions;
let mut file = OpenOptions::new()
    .read(true)
    .write(true)
    .create(true)
    .open("example-lock")?;
let mut lock = file_guard::lock(&mut file, Lock::Exclusive, 0, 1)?;
write_to_file(&mut lock)?;
// the lock will be unlocked when it goes out of scope
```
You can store one or more locks in a struct:

```
use file_guard::{FileGuard, Lock};
use std::fs::{File, OpenOptions};
let file = OpenOptions::new()
    .read(true)
    .write(true)
    .create(true)
    .open("example-lock")?;
struct Thing<'file> {
    a: FileGuard<&'file File>,
    b: FileGuard<&'file File>,
}
let t = Thing {
    a: file_guard::lock(&file, Lock::Exclusive, 0, 1)?,
    b: file_guard::lock(&file, Lock::Shared, 1, 2)?,
};
// both locks will be unlocked when t goes out of scope
```
Anything that can `Deref` or `DerefMut` to a `File` can be used with the [ FileGuard](https://docs.rs/struct.FileGuard.html)
(i.e.

`Rc<File>`):```
use file_guard::{FileGuard, Lock};
use std::fs::{File, OpenOptions};
use std::rc::Rc;
let file = Rc::new(
    OpenOptions::new()
        .read(true)
        .write(true)
        .create(true)
        .open("example-lock")?
);
struct Thing {
    a: FileGuard<Rc<File>>,
    b: FileGuard<Rc<File>>,
}
let t = Thing {
    a: file_guard::lock(file.clone(), Lock::Exclusive, 0, 1)?,
    b: file_guard::lock(file, Lock::Shared, 1, 2)?,
};
// both locks will be unlocked and the file will be closed when t goes out of scope
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [os](https://docs.rs/os/index.html)
- Provides low-level support operations for file locking.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [File](https://docs.rs/struct.FileGuard.html)- Guard
- An RAII implementation of a “scoped lock” of a file. When this structure is dropped (falls out of scope), the lock will be unlocked.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Lock](https://docs.rs/enum.Lock.html)
- The type of a lock operation.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [lock](https://docs.rs/fn.lock.html)
- Wait and claim the desired `Lock`
- [lock_](https://docs.rs/fn.lock_any.html)- any
- First attempt to claim an `Exclusive``Shared`
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_lock.html)- lock
- Attempt to claim the desired `Lock`

# file-guard

A cross-platform library for simple advisory file locking in Rust.

Take a look at the [Documentation](https://docs.rs/file-guard/) for details!

The lock supports both exclusive and shared locking modes for a byte range
of an opened `File` object. Exclusively locking a portion of a file denies
all other processes both shared and exclusive access to the specified
region of the file. Shared locking a portion of a file denies all processes
exclusive access to the specified region of the file. The locked range does
not need to exist within the file, and the ranges may be used for any
arbitrary advisory locking protocol between processes.

The result of a [ lock()](https://docs.rs/file-guard/0.1.0/file_guard/fn.lock.html),

[, or](https://docs.rs/file-guard/0.1.0/file_guard/fn.try_lock.html)

`try_lock()`[is a](https://docs.rs/file-guard/0.1.0/file_guard/fn.lock_any.html)

`lock_any()`[. When dropped, this](https://docs.rs/file-guard/0.1.0/file_guard/struct.FileGuard.html)

`FileGuard`[will unlock the region of the file currently held. Exclusive locks may be](https://docs.rs/file-guard/0.1.0/file_guard/struct.FileGuard.html)

`FileGuard`['ed to either a shared lock cross platform.](https://docs.rs/file-guard/0.1.0/file_guard/struct.FileGuard.html#method.downgrade)

`.downgrade()`On Unix systems `fcntl` is used to perform the locking, and on Windows, `LockFileEx`.
All generally available behavior is consistent across platforms. For platform-
specific behavior, traits may be used for the respective platform. For example,
on Windows, locks cannot be safely upgraded, whereas on Unix systems, this can
be done safely and atomically. To use this feature, the
[ file_guard::os::unix::FileGuardExt](https://docs.rs/file-guard/0.1.0/file_guard/os/unix/trait.FileGuardExt.html) may

`use`ed, enabling the [and](https://docs.rs/file-guard/0.1.0/file_guard/os/unix/trait.FileGuardExt.html#tymethod.upgrade)

`.upgrade()`[methods.](https://docs.rs/file-guard/0.1.0/file_guard/os/unix/trait.FileGuardExt.html#tymethod.try_upgrade)

`.try_upgrade()`Note that on Windows, the file must be open with write permissions to lock it.

# Examples

```
use Lock;
use OpenOptions;
let mut file = new
    .read
    .write
    .create
    .open?;
let mut lock = lock?;
write_to_file?;
// the lock will be unlocked when it goes out of scope
```
You can store one or more locks in a struct:

```
use ;
use ;
let file = new
    .read
    .write
    .create
    .open?;
let t = Thing ;
// both locks will be unlocked when t goes out of scope
```
Anything that can `Deref` or `DerefMut` to a `File` can be used with the [ FileGuard](https://docs.rs/file-guard/0.1.0/file_guard/struct.FileGuard.html).
This works with

`Rc<File>`:```
use ;
use ;
use Rc;
let file = new;
let t = Thing ;
// both locks will be unlocked and the file will be closed when t goes out of scope
```

# vmap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/vmap/^0.6/

## Expand description

A cross-platform library for fast and safe memory-mapped IO and boundary-free ring buffer.

This library defines a convenient API for reading and writing to files
using the hosts virtual memory system, as well as allocating memory and
creating circular memory regions. The design of the API strives to
both minimize the frequency of mapping system calls while still retaining
safe access. Critically, it never attempts the own the `File` object used
for mapping. That is, it never clones it or in any way retains it. While
this has some implications for the API (i.e. [ .flush()](https://docs.rs/struct.MapMut.html#method.flush)), it cannot cause
bugs outside of this library through

`File`’s leaky abstraction when cloned
and then closed.The [ Map](https://docs.rs/struct.Map.html) and

[types are primary means for allocating virtual memory regions, both for a file and anonymously. Generally, the](https://docs.rs/struct.MapMut.html)

`MapMut`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Map.html#method.with_options)

`Map::with_options()`[are used to specify the mapping requirements. See](https://docs.rs/struct.MapMut.html#method.with_options)

`MapMut::with_options()`[for more information.](https://docs.rs/struct.Options.html)

`Options`The [ MapMut](https://docs.rs/struct.MapMut.html) type maintains interior mutability for the mapped memory,
while the

[is read-only. However, it is possible to convert between these types (](https://docs.rs/struct.Map.html)

`Map`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Map.html#method.into_map_mut)

`.into_map_mut()`[) assuming the proper](https://docs.rs/struct.MapMut.html#method.into_map)

`.into_map()`[are specified.](https://docs.rs/struct.Options.html)

`Options`Additionally, a variety of buffer implementations are provided in the
[ vmap::io](https://docs.rs/io/index.html) module. The

[and](https://docs.rs/io/struct.Ring.html)

`Ring`[use cross-platform optimzed circular memory mapping to remove the typical boundary problem with most circular buffers. This ensures all ranges of the underlying byte buffer can be viewed as a single byte slice, event when the value wraps back around to the beginning of the buffer. The](https://docs.rs/io/struct.InfiniteRing.html)

`InfiniteRing`[and](https://docs.rs/io/struct.BufReader.html)

`BufReader`[implement buffered I/O using a](https://docs.rs/io/struct.BufWriter.html)

`BufWriter`[as a backing layer.](https://docs.rs/io/struct.Ring.html)

`Ring`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use vmap::Map;
use std::path::PathBuf;
use std::str::from_utf8;
let path: PathBuf = /* path to file */
// Map the first 4 bytes
let (map, file) = Map::with_options().len(4).open(&path)?;
assert_eq!(Ok("this"), from_utf8(&map[..]));
// Reuse the file to map a different region
let map = Map::with_options().offset(10).len(4).map(&file)?;
assert_eq!(Ok("test"), from_utf8(&map[..]));
```
If opened properly, the `Map` can be moved into a `MapMut` and modifications
to the underlying file can be performed:

```
use vmap::{Map, Flush};
use std::path::PathBuf;
use std::str::from_utf8;
let path: PathBuf = /* path to file */
// Open with write permissions so the Map can be converted into a MapMut
let (map, file) = Map::with_options().write().len(14).open(&path)?;
assert_eq!(Ok("this is a test"), from_utf8(&map[..]));
// Move the Map into a MapMut
// ... we could have started with MapMut::with_options()
let mut map = map.into_map_mut()?;
map[..4].clone_from_slice(b"that");
// Flush the changes to disk synchronously
map.flush(&file, Flush::Sync)?;
// Move the MapMut back into a Map
let map = map.into_map()?;
assert_eq!(Ok("that is a test"), from_utf8(&map[..]));
```
This library contains a [ Ring](https://docs.rs/io/struct.Ring.html) that constructs a circular memory
allocation where values can wrap from around from the end of the buffer back
to the beginning with sequential memory addresses. The

[is similar, however it allows writes to overwrite reads.](https://docs.rs/io/struct.InfiniteRing.html)

`InfiniteRing````
use vmap::io::{Ring, SeqWrite};
use std::io::{BufRead, Read, Write};
let mut buf = Ring::new(4000).unwrap();
let mut i = 1;
// Fill up the buffer with lines.
while buf.write_len() > 20 {
    write!(&mut buf, "this is test line {}\n", i)?;
    i += 1;
}
// No more space is available.
assert!(write!(&mut buf, "this is test line {}\n", i).is_err());
let mut line = String::new();
// Read the first line written.
let len = buf.read_line(&mut line)?;
assert_eq!(line, "this is test line 1\n");
line.clear();
// Read the second line written.
let len = buf.read_line(&mut line)?;
assert_eq!(line, "this is test line 2\n");
// Now there is enough space to write more.
write!(&mut buf, "this is test line {}\n", i)?;
```

# file_guard - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/file-guard/latest/target-redirect/file_guard/

## Expand description

A cross-platform library for simple advisory file locking.

The lock supports both exclusive and shared locking modes for a byte range
of an opened `File` object. Exclusively locking a portion of a file denies
all other processes both shared and exclusive access to the specified
region of the file. Shared locking a portion of a file denies all processes
exclusive access to the specified region of the file. The locked range does
not need to exist within the file, and the ranges may be used for any
arbitrary advisory locking protocol between processes.

The result of a [ lock()](https://docs.rs/fn.lock.html),

[, or](https://docs.rs/fn.try_lock.html)

`try_lock()`[is a](https://docs.rs/fn.lock_any.html)

`lock_any()`[. When dropped, this](https://docs.rs/struct.FileGuard.html)

`FileGuard`[will unlock the region of the file currently held. Exclusive locks may be](https://docs.rs/struct.FileGuard.html)

`FileGuard`[’ed to either a shared lock cross platform.](https://docs.rs/struct.FileGuard.html#method.downgrade)

`.downgrade()`On Unix systems `fcntl` is used to perform the locking, and on Windows, `LockFileEx`.
All generally available behavior is consistent across platforms. For platform-
specific behavior, traits may be used for the respective platform. For example,
on Windows, locks cannot be safely upgraded, whereas on Unix systems, this can
be done safely and atomically. To use this feature, the
[ file_guard::os::unix::FileGuardExt](https://docs.rs/os/unix/trait.FileGuardExt.html) may

`use`ed, enabling the [and](https://docs.rs/os/unix/trait.FileGuardExt.html#tymethod.upgrade)

`.upgrade()`[methods.](https://docs.rs/os/unix/trait.FileGuardExt.html#tymethod.try_upgrade)

`.try_upgrade()`Note that on Windows, the file must be open with write permissions to lock it.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use file_guard::Lock;
use std::fs::OpenOptions;
let mut file = OpenOptions::new()
    .read(true)
    .write(true)
    .create(true)
    .open("example-lock")?;
let mut lock = file_guard::lock(&mut file, Lock::Exclusive, 0, 1)?;
write_to_file(&mut lock)?;
// the lock will be unlocked when it goes out of scope
```
You can store one or more locks in a struct:

```
use file_guard::{FileGuard, Lock};
use std::fs::{File, OpenOptions};
let file = OpenOptions::new()
    .read(true)
    .write(true)
    .create(true)
    .open("example-lock")?;
struct Thing<'file> {
    a: FileGuard<&'file File>,
    b: FileGuard<&'file File>,
}
let t = Thing {
    a: file_guard::lock(&file, Lock::Exclusive, 0, 1)?,
    b: file_guard::lock(&file, Lock::Shared, 1, 2)?,
};
// both locks will be unlocked when t goes out of scope
```
Anything that can `Deref` or `DerefMut` to a `File` can be used with the [ FileGuard](https://docs.rs/struct.FileGuard.html)
(i.e.

`Rc<File>`):```
use file_guard::{FileGuard, Lock};
use std::fs::{File, OpenOptions};
use std::rc::Rc;
let file = Rc::new(
    OpenOptions::new()
        .read(true)
        .write(true)
        .create(true)
        .open("example-lock")?
);
struct Thing {
    a: FileGuard<Rc<File>>,
    b: FileGuard<Rc<File>>,
}
let t = Thing {
    a: file_guard::lock(file.clone(), Lock::Exclusive, 0, 1)?,
    b: file_guard::lock(file, Lock::Shared, 1, 2)?,
};
// both locks will be unlocked and the file will be closed when t goes out of scope
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [os](https://docs.rs/os/index.html)
- Provides low-level support operations for file locking.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [File](https://docs.rs/struct.FileGuard.html)- Guard
- An RAII implementation of a “scoped lock” of a file. When this structure is dropped (falls out of scope), the lock will be unlocked.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Lock](https://docs.rs/enum.Lock.html)
- The type of a lock operation.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [lock](https://docs.rs/fn.lock.html)
- Wait and claim the desired `Lock`
- [lock_](https://docs.rs/fn.lock_any.html)- any
- First attempt to claim an `Exclusive``Shared`
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_lock.html)- lock
- Attempt to claim the desired `Lock`

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# texform_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/texform-core/0.2.0/texform_core/

## Expand description

TeXForm core library — LaTeX formula parsing, AST, and transformation.

[§](https://docs.rs#modules)Modules

| Module | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `parse` | : the main API for configuring knowledge and parsing`ParseContext` |
| `ast` | Mutable arena-backed AST for tree transforms |
| `lexer` | Logos-based lexer mapping LaTeX source to tokens |
| `column_parser` | Standalone parser for `{lcc}`column specifications |

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules-1)

- [ast](https://docs.rs/ast/index.html)
- Transform-ready mutable AST for tree editing.
- [column_](https://docs.rs/column_parser/index.html)- parser
- Column template parser aligned with MathJax ColumnParser semantics.
- [document](https://docs.rs/document/index.html)
- Public, fallible DOM layer over the internal panic-contract `Ast`
- [knowledge](https://docs.rs/knowledge/index.html)
- Knowledge base: the backing store behind `ParseContext`
- [lexer](https://docs.rs/lexer/index.html)
- LaTeX lexical analysis powered by [Logos](https://docs.rs/logos).
- [parse](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)
- [serialize](https://docs.rs/serialize/index.html)
- Canonical AST serializer — converts `Ast`
- [target_](https://docs.rs/target_counter/index.html)- counter
- Target occurrence counting for parsed TeXForm syntax trees.

# arcx-cli 0.1.8 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/arcx-cli/0.1.8

# arcx-cli

CLI scaffolding tool for **Arcx** — a convention-over-configuration web framework for Rust.

## Install

```
```
## Commands

### Create a new project

```
```
Generated structure:

```
myapp/
├── src/
│   ├── main.rs
│   ├── router.rs
│   ├── prelude.rs
│   ├── controller/
│   │   └── home.rs
│   ├── middleware/
│   ├── service/
│   │   ├── mod.rs        # services! container
│   │   └── user.rs
│   ├── schedule/
│   └── helper/
│       └── response.rs
├── config/
│   ├── config.default.toml
│   └── config.prod.toml
└── Cargo.toml
```
### Generate code (auto-register)

All generators automatically register into the appropriate files — zero manual wiring.

```
# Generate controller (alias: g c)
# → Creates src/controller/user.rs
# → Auto-registers in controller/mod.rs + router.rs
# Generate service (alias: g s)
# → Creates src/service/order.rs
# → Auto-registers in service/mod.rs (services! macro)
# Generate middleware (alias: g m)
# → Creates src/middleware/rate_limit.rs (Ctx + Next + ReqParts signature)
# → Auto-registers in middleware/mod.rs
# Generate schedule job (alias: g j)
# → Creates src/schedule/cleanup.rs
# → Auto-registers in schedule/mod.rs + main.rs (.schedule())
```
### Development server (hot reload)

```
```
Watches file changes, recompiles, and restarts automatically.

### Project info

```
```
## Configuration

Each middleware/feature manages its own config section:

```
# config/config.default.toml
[]
 = 3000
[]
 = true
 = ["*"]
[]
 = true
[]
 = true
 = false
```
Rule: **has section +  enable = true = on.** No section or

`enable = false` = off.## Links

- [GitHub](https://github.com/name-q/Arcx)
- [arcx-core](https://crates.io/crates/arcx-core)— Framework core library
- [arcx-macros](https://crates.io/crates/arcx-macros)— Proc macros

# aerocontext_leidos - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/aerocontext-leidos/0.4.5/aerocontext_leidos/

## Expand description

[ aerocontext_core::WeatherBriefingProvider](https://docs.rs/aerocontext-core/0.4.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aerocontext_core/weather/trait.WeatherBriefingProvider.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/aerocontext-core/0.4.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aerocontext_core/notam/trait.NotamProvider.html)

`aerocontext_core::NotamProvider`[, and](https://docs.rs/aerocontext-core/0.4.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aerocontext_core/tfr/trait.TfrProvider.html)

`aerocontext_core::TfrProvider`[adapter for the Leidos Flight Service (1800wxbrief) Pilot Web Service.](https://docs.rs/aerocontext-core/0.4.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aerocontext_core/route_alert/trait.RouteAlertProvider.html)

`aerocontext_core::RouteAlertProvider`Speaks the FFSP REST API (form-urlencoded `POST` to
`FP/areaBriefing` / `FP/routeBriefing`), returning
a `SIMPLE` briefing for a circular area around a fix or coordinate,
authenticated with pre-emptive HTTP Basic vendor credentials. Requests
are sent with `notABriefing=true` — data retrieval only, with no pilot
association and no historical retention. NOTAMs are extracted from the same
`SIMPLE` narrative as low-fidelity records for cross-source reconciliation.
[ LeidosClient::area_briefing_pdf](https://docs.rs/struct.LeidosClient.html#method.area_briefing_pdf) requests the same area as an NGBv2
briefing (

`briefingResultFormat=PDF`) and returns the vendor-composed
standard briefing as decoded PDF bytes.
Recorded pilot briefings (`webUserName` + `aircraftIdentifier` +
service-provider authorization) are a future extension.Independent, unofficial adapter (test server only) — not affiliated with or endorsed by Leidos or the FAA.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Leidos](https://docs.rs/struct.LeidosClient.html)- Client
- Leidos FFSP Pilot Web Service client.
- [Leidos](https://docs.rs/struct.LeidosConfig.html)- Config
- Configuration for `LeidosClient`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Config](https://docs.rs/enum.ConfigError.html)- Error
- Failure constructing a `LeidosClient`

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [TEST_](https://docs.rs/constant.TEST_ENDPOINT.html)- ENDPOINT
- Leidos evaluation/test (ffspelabs) REST base. Resource paths
(`FP/areaBriefing`,`FP/routeBriefing`, …) are appended to it. This is the only endpoint this adapter targets; production 1800wxbrief is not wired.

# aerocontext_nms - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/aerocontext-nms/0.4.5/aerocontext_nms/

## Expand description

FAA NOTAM Management System (NMS-API) NOTAM source for `aerocontext-core`.

[ NmsClient](https://docs.rs/struct.NmsClient.html) implements

[: it authenticates with OAuth2](https://docs.rs/aerocontext-core/0.4.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aerocontext_core/notam/trait.NotamProvider.html)

`aerocontext_core::NotamProvider``client_credentials` (an FAA-issued client id and
secret, env-only and never persisted), queries `/v1/notams` in GeoJSON, and
maps each NOTAM onto a provider-neutral [. It “packs what the vendor has”; assembling and cross-checking against other sources is](https://docs.rs/aerocontext-core/0.4.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aerocontext_core/notam/struct.NotamRecord.html)

`aerocontext_core::NotamRecord`[’s job, not this crate’s.](https://docs.rs/aerocontext-core/0.4.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aerocontext_core/notam/reconcile/fn.reconcile.html)

`aerocontext_core::reconcile`Defaults target the FAA **staging** environment; production is two env
overrides ([ BASE_URL_ENV](https://docs.rs/constant.BASE_URL_ENV.html) /

[), not a code change.](https://docs.rs/constant.AUTH_URL_ENV.html)

`AUTH_URL_ENV`Independent, unofficial adapter — not affiliated with or endorsed by the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration.

- Optional environment override for the API base URL (default: staging).

- Environment variable holding the FAA-issued client id.

- Environment variable holding the FAA-issued client secret.

# aerocontext_awc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/aerocontext-awc/0.4.5/aerocontext_awc/

## Expand description

[ aerocontext_core::WeatherBriefingProvider](https://docs.rs/aerocontext-core/0.4.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aerocontext_core/weather/trait.WeatherBriefingProvider.html) adapter for the
aviationweather.gov Data API.

The Data API is product-oriented: an area briefing fans out over the
per-product endpoints (`metar`, `taf`, `pirep`, `airsigmet`) under
`https://aviationweather.gov/api/data/` and normalizes the JSON
responses into [ aerocontext_core::Product](https://docs.rs/aerocontext-core/0.4.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aerocontext_core/model/struct.Product.html)s. No authentication is
required, but AWC asks clients to send a custom

`User-Agent`.Independent, unofficial adapter — not affiliated with or endorsed by the NOAA/NWS Aviation Weather Center.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [AwcClient](https://docs.rs/struct.AwcClient.html)
- aviationweather.gov Data API client.
- [AwcConfig](https://docs.rs/struct.AwcConfig.html)
- Configuration for `AwcClient`
- [Route](https://docs.rs/struct.RouteFanout.html)- Fanout
- The fan-out shape of an AWC route briefing: `segments * kinds`upstream requests, one per corridor bounding box per product kind.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Config](https://docs.rs/enum.ConfigError.html)- Error
- Failure constructing an `AwcClient`

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_BASE_URL.html)- BASE_ - URL
- Production base URL of the Data API.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [route_](https://docs.rs/fn.route_fanout.html)- fanout
- Predict the fan-out `AwcClient::route_briefing``request`—`segments * kinds`sequential upstream requests. Lets a caller (e.g. an agent-facing tool fed untrusted input) refuse an oversized request before issuing a single call.

# sokgi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sokgi/0.2.0/sokgi/

## Expand description

Canonicalize GCC-style compiler flags for content hashing.

```
use sokgi::{Dialect, FlagSet};
let (set, _) = FlagSet::parse("-O3 -O2 -g", Dialect::C).unwrap();
assert_eq!(set.canonical(), "-O2 -g");
```

# aerocontext_planning - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/aerocontext-planning/0.4.5/aerocontext_planning/

## Expand description

Flight-route planning: the single engine that turns a route or a flight plan into usable geometry.

Every frontend — the `aerocontext` CLI, the MCP `route_brief` tool, a
future GUI or iOS app — composes this crate rather than reimplementing
any of it. The hub is the [ flightplan::FlightPlan](https://docs.rs/flightplan/struct.FlightPlan.html) domain model;
Garmin

`.fpl` is one *codec*(inside

[), not the privileged format, so other formats slot in beside it without touching planning logic.](https://docs.rs/flightplan/index.html)

`flightplan`The pieces:

- `flightplan`- `FlightPlan`model and its- `.fpl`codec.
- `route`- `NavDataSnapshot`
- `corridor`
- `crosssection`- `AircraftProfile`

This crate consumes the cycle-stamped snapshot that `aerocontext-navdata`
produces; it never fetches or distributes data itself.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use corridor::`- [Corridor](https://docs.rs/corridor/struct.Corridor.html);

# file-guard 0.2.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/file-guard/0.2.0

# file-guard

A cross-platform library for simple advisory file locking in Rust.

Take a look at the [Documentation](https://docs.rs/file-guard/) for details!

The lock supports both exclusive and shared locking modes for a byte range
of an opened `File` object. Exclusively locking a portion of a file denies
all other processes both shared and exclusive access to the specified
region of the file. Shared locking a portion of a file denies all processes
exclusive access to the specified region of the file. The locked range does
not need to exist within the file, and the ranges may be used for any
arbitrary advisory locking protocol between processes.

The result of a [ lock()](https://docs.rs/file-guard/0.1.0/file_guard/fn.lock.html),

[, or](https://docs.rs/file-guard/0.1.0/file_guard/fn.try_lock.html)

`try_lock()`[is a](https://docs.rs/file-guard/0.1.0/file_guard/fn.lock_any.html)

`lock_any()`[. When dropped, this](https://docs.rs/file-guard/0.1.0/file_guard/struct.FileGuard.html)

`FileGuard`[will unlock the region of the file currently held. Exclusive locks may be](https://docs.rs/file-guard/0.1.0/file_guard/struct.FileGuard.html)

`FileGuard`['ed to either a shared lock cross platform.](https://docs.rs/file-guard/0.1.0/file_guard/struct.FileGuard.html#method.downgrade)

`.downgrade()`On Unix systems `fcntl` is used to perform the locking, and on Windows, `LockFileEx`.
All generally available behavior is consistent across platforms. For platform-
specific behavior, traits may be used for the respective platform. For example,
on Windows, locks cannot be safely upgraded, whereas on Unix systems, this can
be done safely and atomically. To use this feature, the
[ file_guard::os::unix::FileGuardExt](https://docs.rs/file-guard/0.1.0/file_guard/os/unix/trait.FileGuardExt.html) may

`use`ed, enabling the [and](https://docs.rs/file-guard/0.1.0/file_guard/os/unix/trait.FileGuardExt.html#tymethod.upgrade)

`.upgrade()`[methods.](https://docs.rs/file-guard/0.1.0/file_guard/os/unix/trait.FileGuardExt.html#tymethod.try_upgrade)

`.try_upgrade()`Note that on Windows, the file must be open with write permissions to lock it.

# Examples

```
use Lock;
use OpenOptions;
let mut file = new
    .read
    .write
    .create
    .open?;
let mut lock = lock?;
write_to_file?;
// the lock will be unlocked when it goes out of scope
```
You can store one or more locks in a struct:

```
use ;
use ;
let file = new
    .read
    .write
    .create
    .open?;
let t = Thing ;
// both locks will be unlocked when t goes out of scope
```
Anything that can `Deref` or `DerefMut` to a `File` can be used with the [ FileGuard](https://docs.rs/file-guard/0.1.0/file_guard/struct.FileGuard.html).
This works with

`Rc<File>`:```
use ;
use ;
use Rc;
let file = new;
let t = Thing ;
// both locks will be unlocked and the file will be closed when t goes out of scope
```

# file_guard - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/file-guard/0.2.0/target-redirect/file_guard/

## Expand description

A cross-platform library for simple advisory file locking.

The lock supports both exclusive and shared locking modes for a byte range
of an opened `File` object. Exclusively locking a portion of a file denies
all other processes both shared and exclusive access to the specified
region of the file. Shared locking a portion of a file denies all processes
exclusive access to the specified region of the file. The locked range does
not need to exist within the file, and the ranges may be used for any
arbitrary advisory locking protocol between processes.

The result of a [ lock()](https://docs.rs/fn.lock.html),

[, or](https://docs.rs/fn.try_lock.html)

`try_lock()`[is a](https://docs.rs/fn.lock_any.html)

`lock_any()`[. When dropped, this](https://docs.rs/struct.FileGuard.html)

`FileGuard`[will unlock the region of the file currently held. Exclusive locks may be](https://docs.rs/struct.FileGuard.html)

`FileGuard`[’ed to either a shared lock cross platform.](https://docs.rs/struct.FileGuard.html#method.downgrade)

`.downgrade()`On Unix systems `fcntl` is used to perform the locking, and on Windows, `LockFileEx`.
All generally available behavior is consistent across platforms. For platform-
specific behavior, traits may be used for the respective platform. For example,
on Windows, locks cannot be safely upgraded, whereas on Unix systems, this can
be done safely and atomically. To use this feature, the
[ file_guard::os::unix::FileGuardExt](https://docs.rs/os/unix/trait.FileGuardExt.html) may

`use`ed, enabling the [and](https://docs.rs/os/unix/trait.FileGuardExt.html#tymethod.upgrade)

`.upgrade()`[methods.](https://docs.rs/os/unix/trait.FileGuardExt.html#tymethod.try_upgrade)

`.try_upgrade()`Note that on Windows, the file must be open with write permissions to lock it.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use file_guard::Lock;
use std::fs::OpenOptions;
let mut file = OpenOptions::new()
    .read(true)
    .write(true)
    .create(true)
    .open("example-lock")?;
let mut lock = file_guard::lock(&mut file, Lock::Exclusive, 0, 1)?;
write_to_file(&mut lock)?;
// the lock will be unlocked when it goes out of scope
```
You can store one or more locks in a struct:

```
use file_guard::{FileGuard, Lock};
use std::fs::{File, OpenOptions};
let file = OpenOptions::new()
    .read(true)
    .write(true)
    .create(true)
    .open("example-lock")?;
struct Thing<'file> {
    a: FileGuard<&'file File>,
    b: FileGuard<&'file File>,
}
let t = Thing {
    a: file_guard::lock(&file, Lock::Exclusive, 0, 1)?,
    b: file_guard::lock(&file, Lock::Shared, 1, 2)?,
};
// both locks will be unlocked when t goes out of scope
```
Anything that can `Deref` or `DerefMut` to a `File` can be used with the [ FileGuard](https://docs.rs/struct.FileGuard.html)
(i.e.

`Rc<File>`):```
use file_guard::{FileGuard, Lock};
use std::fs::{File, OpenOptions};
use std::rc::Rc;
let file = Rc::new(
    OpenOptions::new()
        .read(true)
        .write(true)
        .create(true)
        .open("example-lock")?
);
struct Thing {
    a: FileGuard<Rc<File>>,
    b: FileGuard<Rc<File>>,
}
let t = Thing {
    a: file_guard::lock(file.clone(), Lock::Exclusive, 0, 1)?,
    b: file_guard::lock(file, Lock::Shared, 1, 2)?,
};
// both locks will be unlocked and the file will be closed when t goes out of scope
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [os](https://docs.rs/os/index.html)
- Provides low-level support operations for file locking.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [File](https://docs.rs/struct.FileGuard.html)- Guard
- An RAII implementation of a “scoped lock” of a file. When this structure is dropped (falls out of scope), the lock will be unlocked.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Lock](https://docs.rs/enum.Lock.html)
- The type of a lock operation.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [lock](https://docs.rs/fn.lock.html)
- Wait and claim the desired `Lock`
- [lock_](https://docs.rs/fn.lock_any.html)- any
- First attempt to claim an `Exclusive``Shared`
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_lock.html)- lock
- Attempt to claim the desired `Lock`

[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!         .open("example-lock")?
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! );
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//!
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! struct Thing {
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//!     a: FileGuard<Rc<File>>,
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//!     b: FileGuard<Rc<File>>,
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! }
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//!
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! let t = Thing {
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//!     a: file_guard::lock(file.clone(), Lock::Exclusive, 0, 1)?,
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//!     b: file_guard::lock(file, Lock::Shared, 1, 2)?,
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! };
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! // both locks will be unlocked and the file will be closed when t goes out of scope
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! # Ok(())
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! # }
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! ```

[124](https://docs.rs#124)/// The type of a lock operation.
[125](https://docs.rs#125)///
[126](https://docs.rs#126)/// This is used to specify the desired lock type when used with [`lock()`]
[127](https://docs.rs#127)/// and [`try_lock()`], and it is the successful result type returned by
[128](https://docs.rs#128)/// [`lock_any()`].
[129](https://docs.rs#129)///
[130](https://docs.rs#130)/// [`lock()`]: fn.lock.html
[131](https://docs.rs#131)/// [`try_lock()`]: fn.try_lock.html
[132](https://docs.rs#132)/// [`lock_any()`]: fn.lock_any.html
[133](https://docs.rs#133)#[derive(Copy, Clone, PartialEq, Debug)]
[134](https://docs.rs#134)pub enum Lock {
[135](https://docs.rs#135)    /// A shared lock may be concurrently held by multiple processes while
[136](https://docs.rs#136)    /// preventing future exclusive locks its lifetime.
[137](https://docs.rs#137)    ///
[138](https://docs.rs#138)    /// The shared lock type cannot be obtained while an exclusive lock is held
[139](https://docs.rs#139)    /// by another process. When successful, a shared lock guarantees that only
[140](https://docs.rs#140)    /// one or more shared locks are concurrently held, and that no exclusive
[141](https://docs.rs#141)    /// locks are held.
[142](https://docs.rs#142)    ///
[143](https://docs.rs#143)    /// This lock type--often referred to as a read lock--may be used as a
[144](https://docs.rs#144)    /// means of signaling read integrity. When used cooperatively, they ensure
[145](https://docs.rs#145)    /// no exclusive lock is held, and thus, no other process may be writing to
[146](https://docs.rs#146)    /// a shared resource.
[147](https://docs.rs#147)    Shared,
[148](https://docs.rs#148)    /// An exclusive lock may only be held by a single process.
[149](https://docs.rs#149)    ///
[150](https://docs.rs#150)    /// The exclusive lock type can neither be obtained while any shared locks
[151](https://docs.rs#151)    /// are held or while any other exclusive locks are held. This linearizes
[152](https://docs.rs#152)    /// the sequence of processes attempting to acquire an exclusive lock.
[153](https://docs.rs#153)    ///
[154](https://docs.rs#154)    /// This lock type--also known as a write lock--may be used as a means of
[155](https://docs.rs#155)    /// ensuring write exclusivity. In a cooperative locking environment, all
[156](https://docs.rs#156)    /// access to a shared resource is halted until the exlusive lock is
[157](https://docs.rs#157)    /// released.
[158](https://docs.rs#158)    Exclusive,
[159](https://docs.rs#159)}
[160](https://docs.rs#160)
[161](https://docs.rs#161)/// Wait and claim the desired [`Lock`] type using a byte range of a file.
[162](https://docs.rs#162)///
[163](https://docs.rs#163)/// The byte range does not need to exist in the underlying file.
[164](https://docs.rs#164)///
[165](https://docs.rs#165)/// [`Lock`]: enum.Lock.html
[166](https://docs.rs#166)pub fn lock<T: Deref<Target = File>>(

[171](https://docs.rs#171)) -> io::Result<FileGuard<T>> {
[172](https://docs.rs#172)    unsafe {
[173](https://docs.rs#173)        raw_file_lock(&file, Some(lock), offset, len, true)?;
[174](https://docs.rs#174)    }
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    Ok(FileGuard {
[176](https://docs.rs#176)        offset,
[177](https://docs.rs#177)        len,
[178](https://docs.rs#178)        file,

[180](https://docs.rs#180)    })

[186](https://docs.rs#186)/// `Error` of kind `ErrorKind::WouldBlock` is returned. Otherwise if

[192](https://docs.rs#192)pub fn try_lock<T: Deref<Target = File>>(

[209](https://docs.rs#209)/// First attempt to claim an [`Exclusive`] lock and then fallback to a
[210](https://docs.rs#210)/// [`Shared`] lock for a byte range of a file. This is not currently an
[211](https://docs.rs#211)/// atomic operation.
[212](https://docs.rs#212)///
[213](https://docs.rs#213)/// When successful, the [`FileGuard`] may be inspected for the lock type
[214](https://docs.rs#214)/// obtained using [`.lock_type()`], [`.is_shared()`], or [`.is_exclusive()`].
[215](https://docs.rs#215)///
[216](https://docs.rs#216)/// The byte range does not need to exist in the underlying file.
[217](https://docs.rs#217)///
[218](https://docs.rs#218)/// [`Exclusive`]: enum.Lock.html#variant.Exclusive
[219](https://docs.rs#219)/// [`Shared`]: enum.Lock.html#variant.Shared
[220](https://docs.rs#220)/// [`FileGuard`]: struct.FileGuard.html
[221](https://docs.rs#221)/// [`.lock_type()`]: struct.FileGuard.html#method.lock_type
[222](https://docs.rs#222)/// [`.is_shared()`]: struct.FileGuard.html#method.is_shared
[223](https://docs.rs#223)/// [`.is_exclusive()`]: struct.FileGuard.html#method.is_exclusive
[224](https://docs.rs#224)pub fn lock_any<T: Deref<Target = File>>(
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    file: T,
[226](https://docs.rs#226)    offset: usize,
[227](https://docs.rs#227)    len: usize,
[228](https://docs.rs#228)) -> io::Result<FileGuard<T>> {
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    let lock = match unsafe { raw_file_lock(&file, Some(Lock::Exclusive), offset, len, false) } {
[230](https://docs.rs#230)        Ok(_) => Lock::Exclusive,
[231](https://docs.rs#231)        Err(e) => {
[232](https://docs.rs#232)            if e.kind() == ErrorKind::WouldBlock {
[233](https://docs.rs#233)                unsafe {
[234](https://docs.rs#234)                    raw_file_lock(&file, Some(Lock::Shared), offset, len, true)?;
[235](https://docs.rs#235)                }
[236](https://docs.rs#236)                Lock::Shared
[237](https://docs.rs#237)            } else {
[238](https://docs.rs#238)                return Err(e);
[239](https://docs.rs#239)            }
[240](https://docs.rs#240)        }
[241](https://docs.rs#241)    };
[242](https://docs.rs#242)    Ok(FileGuard {
[243](https://docs.rs#243)        offset,
[244](https://docs.rs#244)        len,
[245](https://docs.rs#245)        file,
[246](https://docs.rs#246)        lock,
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    })
[248](https://docs.rs#248)}

# try_lock in file_guard - Rust

Attempt to claim the desired Lock type using a byte range of a file.

If the desired Lock type cannot be obtained without blocking, an
Error of kind ErrorKind::WouldBlock is returned. Otherwise if
successful, the lock is held.

# FileGuard in file_guard - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/file-guard/0.2.0/file_guard/struct.FileGuard.html

## Expand description

An RAII implementation of a “scoped lock” of a file. When this structure is dropped (falls out of scope), the lock will be unlocked.

This structure is created by the [ lock()](https://docs.rs/fn.lock.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/fn.try_lock.html)

`try_lock()`[functions.](https://docs.rs/fn.lock_any.html)

`lock_any()`## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Safely exchanges an `Exclusive`[ Lock](https://docs.rs/enum.Lock.html) for a

[one.](https://docs.rs/enum.Lock.html#variant.Shared)

`Shared`If the currently held lock is already [ Shared](https://docs.rs/enum.Lock.html#variant.Shared), no change is made and
the method succeeds. This exchange safely ensures no lock is released
during operation. That is, no waiting

[lock attempts may obtain the lock during the downgrade. Other](https://docs.rs/enum.Lock.html#variant.Exclusive)

`Exclusive`[locks waiting will be granted a lock as a result, however.](https://docs.rs/enum.Lock.html#variant.Shared)

# Lock in file_guard - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/file-guard/0.2.0/file_guard/enum.Lock.html

```
pub enum Lock {
    Shared,
    Exclusive,
}
```
## Expand description

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

A shared lock may be concurrently held by multiple processes while preventing future exclusive locks its lifetime.

The shared lock type cannot be obtained while an exclusive lock is held by another process. When successful, a shared lock guarantees that only one or more shared locks are concurrently held, and that no exclusive locks are held.

This lock type–often referred to as a read lock–may be used as a means of signaling read integrity. When used cooperatively, they ensure no exclusive lock is held, and thus, no other process may be writing to a shared resource.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Exclusive)

### Exclusive

An exclusive lock may only be held by a single process.

The exclusive lock type can neither be obtained while any shared locks are held or while any other exclusive locks are held. This linearizes the sequence of processes attempting to acquire an exclusive lock.

This lock type–also known as a write lock–may be used as a means of ensuring write exclusivity. In a cooperative locking environment, all access to a shared resource is halted until the exlusive lock is released.

# file_guard - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/file-guard/latest/file_guard/

## Expand description

A cross-platform library for simple advisory file locking.

The lock supports both exclusive and shared locking modes for a byte range
of an opened `File` object. Exclusively locking a portion of a file denies
all other processes both shared and exclusive access to the specified
region of the file. Shared locking a portion of a file denies all processes
exclusive access to the specified region of the file. The locked range does
not need to exist within the file, and the ranges may be used for any
arbitrary advisory locking protocol between processes.

The result of a [ lock()](https://docs.rs/fn.lock.html),

[, or](https://docs.rs/fn.try_lock.html)

`try_lock()`[is a](https://docs.rs/fn.lock_any.html)

`lock_any()`[. When dropped, this](https://docs.rs/struct.FileGuard.html)

`FileGuard`[will unlock the region of the file currently held. Exclusive locks may be](https://docs.rs/struct.FileGuard.html)

`FileGuard`[’ed to either a shared lock cross platform.](https://docs.rs/struct.FileGuard.html#method.downgrade)

`.downgrade()`On Unix systems `fcntl` is used to perform the locking, and on Windows, `LockFileEx`.
All generally available behavior is consistent across platforms. For platform-
specific behavior, traits may be used for the respective platform. For example,
on Windows, locks cannot be safely upgraded, whereas on Unix systems, this can
be done safely and atomically. To use this feature, the
[ file_guard::os::unix::FileGuardExt](https://docs.rs/os/unix/trait.FileGuardExt.html) may

`use`ed, enabling the [and](https://docs.rs/os/unix/trait.FileGuardExt.html#tymethod.upgrade)

`.upgrade()`[methods.](https://docs.rs/os/unix/trait.FileGuardExt.html#tymethod.try_upgrade)

`.try_upgrade()`Note that on Windows, the file must be open with write permissions to lock it.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use file_guard::Lock;
use std::fs::OpenOptions;
let mut file = OpenOptions::new()
    .read(true)
    .write(true)
    .create(true)
    .open("example-lock")?;
let mut lock = file_guard::lock(&mut file, Lock::Exclusive, 0, 1)?;
write_to_file(&mut lock)?;
// the lock will be unlocked when it goes out of scope
```
You can store one or more locks in a struct:

```
use file_guard::{FileGuard, Lock};
use std::fs::{File, OpenOptions};
let file = OpenOptions::new()
    .read(true)
    .write(true)
    .create(true)
    .open("example-lock")?;
struct Thing<'file> {
    a: FileGuard<&'file File>,
    b: FileGuard<&'file File>,
}
let t = Thing {
    a: file_guard::lock(&file, Lock::Exclusive, 0, 1)?,
    b: file_guard::lock(&file, Lock::Shared, 1, 2)?,
};
// both locks will be unlocked when t goes out of scope
```
Anything that can `Deref` or `DerefMut` to a `File` can be used with the [ FileGuard](https://docs.rs/struct.FileGuard.html)
(i.e.

`Rc<File>`):```
use file_guard::{FileGuard, Lock};
use std::fs::{File, OpenOptions};
use std::rc::Rc;
let file = Rc::new(
    OpenOptions::new()
        .read(true)
        .write(true)
        .create(true)
        .open("example-lock")?
);
struct Thing {
    a: FileGuard<Rc<File>>,
    b: FileGuard<Rc<File>>,
}
let t = Thing {
    a: file_guard::lock(file.clone(), Lock::Exclusive, 0, 1)?,
    b: file_guard::lock(file, Lock::Shared, 1, 2)?,
};
// both locks will be unlocked and the file will be closed when t goes out of scope
```

# vmap 0.6.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/vmap/^0.6

# vmap-rs

A cross-platform library for fast and safe memory-mapped IO and boundary-free ring buffer.

This library defines a convenient API for reading and writing to files
using the hosts virtual memory system, as well as allocating memory and
creating circular memory regions. The design of the API strives to
both minimize the frequency of mapping system calls while still retaining
safe access. Critically, it never attempts the own the `File` object used
for mapping. That is, it never clones it or in any way retains it. While
this has some implications for the API (i.e. [ .flush()](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.MapMut.html#method.flush)), it cannot cause
bugs outside of this library through

`File`'s leaky abstraction when cloned
and then closed.The [ Map](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.Map.html) and

[types are primary means for allocating virtual memory regions, both for a file and anonymously. Generally, the](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.MapMut.html)

`MapMut`[and](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.Map.html#method.with_options)

`Map::with_options()`[are used to specify the mapping requirements. See](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.MapMut.html#method.with_options)

`MapMut::with_options()`[for more information.](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.Options.html)

`Options`The [ MapMut](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.MapMut.html) type maintains interior mutability for the mapped memory,
while the

[is read-only. However, it is possible to convert between these types (](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.Map.html)

`Map`[and](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.Map.html#method.into_map_mut)

`.into_map_mut()`[) assuming the proper](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.MapMut.html#method.into_map)

`.into_map()`[are specified.](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.Options.html)

`Options`Additionally, a variety of buffer implementations are provided in the
[ vmap::io](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/io/index.html) module. The

[and](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/io/struct.Ring.html)

`Ring`[use cross-platform optimzed circular memory mapping to remove the typical boundary problem with most circular buffers. This ensures all ranges of the underlying byte buffer can be viewed as a single byte slice, event when the value wraps back around to the beginning of the buffer. The](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/io/struct.InfiniteRing.html)

`InfiniteRing`[and](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/io/struct.BufReader.html)

`BufReader`[implement buffered I/O using a](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/io/struct.BufWriter.html)

`BufWriter`[as a backing layer.](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/io/struct.Ring.html)

`Ring`Take a look at the [Documentation](https://docs.rs/vmap/) for details!

# Examples

```
use Map;
use ;
let path = "example";
// Write some test data
write?;
// Map the first 4 bytes
let  = with_options.len.open?;
assert_eq!;
// Reuse the file to map a different region
let map = with_options.offset.len.map?;
assert_eq!;
```
If opened properly, the [ Map](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.Map.html) can be moved into a

[and modifications to the underlying file can be performed:](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.MapMut.html)

`MapMut````
use Map;
use ;
let path = "example";
// Write some test data
write?;
// Open with write permissions so the Map can be converted into a MapMut
let  = with_options.write.len.open?;
assert_eq!;
// Move the Map into a MapMut
// ... we could have started with MapMut::with_options()
let mut map = map.into_map_mut?;
map.clone_from_slice;
// Flush the changes to disk synchronously
map.flush?;
// Move the MapMut back into a Map
let map = map.into_map?;
assert_eq!;
```
## Ring Buffer

The [ vmap](https://docs.rs/vmap/) library contains a

[that constructs a circular memory allocation where values can wrap from around from the end of the buffer back to the beginning with sequential memory addresses. The](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/io/struct.Ring.html)

`Ring`[is similar, however it allows writes to overwrite reads.](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/io/struct.InfiniteRing.html)

`InfiniteRing````
use ;
use ;
let mut buf = new.unwrap;
let mut i = 1;
// Fill up the buffer with lines.
while buf.write_len > 20
// No more space is available.
assert!;
let mut line = Stringnew;
// Read the first line written.
let len = buf.read_line?;
assert_eq!;
line.clear;
// Read the second line written.
let len = buf.read_line?;
assert_eq!;
// Now there is enough space to write more.
write!?;
```

# libc 0.2.186 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/libc/^0.2.109

# libc - Raw FFI bindings to platforms' system libraries

`libc` provides all of the definitions necessary to easily interoperate with C
code (or "C-like" code) on each of the platforms that Rust supports. This
includes type definitions (e.g. `c_int`), constants (e.g. `EINVAL`) as well as
function headers (e.g. `malloc`).

This crate exports all underlying platform types, functions, and constants under
the crate root, so all items are accessible as `libc::foo`. The types and values
of all the exported APIs match the platform that libc is compiled for.

Windows API bindings are not included in this crate. If you are looking for
WinAPI bindings, consider using crates like [windows-sys](https://docs.rs/windows-sys).

More detailed information about the design of this library can be found in its
[associated RFC](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/HEAD/text/1291-promote-libc.md).

## v1.0 Roadmap

Currently, `libc` has two active branches: `main` for the upcoming v1.0 release,
and `libc-0.2` for the currently published version. By default all pull requests
should target `main`; once reviewed, they can be cherry picked to the `libc-0.2`
branch if needed.

We will stop making new v0.2 releases once v1.0 is released.

See the section in [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://docs.rs/CONTRIBUTING.md#v10-roadmap) for more
details.

## Usage

Add the following to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.2"
```
## Features

-
`std`: by default`libc`links to the standard library. Disable this feature to remove this dependency and be able to use`libc`in`#![no_std]`crates.
-
`extra_traits`: all`struct`s implemented in`libc`are`Copy`and`Clone`. This feature derives`Debug`,`Eq`,`Hash`, and`PartialEq`.

The following features are deprecated:

- `use_std`: this is equivalent to- `std`
- `const-extern-fn`: this is now enabled by default
- `align`: this is now enabled by default

## Rust version support

The minimum supported Rust toolchain version is currently **Rust 1.65**.

Increases to the MSRV are allowed to change without a major (i.e. semver- breaking) release in order to avoid a ripple effect in the ecosystem. A policy for when this may change is a work in progress.

`libc` may continue to compile with Rust versions older than the current MSRV
but this is not guaranteed.

## Platform support

You can see the platform(target)-specific docs on [docs.rs](https://docs.rs/libc), select a platform
you want to see.

See [ ci/verify-build.py](https://github.com/rust-lang/libc/blob/HEAD/ci/verify-build.py) for
the platforms on which

`libc` is guaranteed to build for each Rust toolchain.
The test matrices at [GitHub Actions](https://github.com/rust-lang/libc/actions)show the platforms in which

`libc` tests
are run.## License

# winapi 0.3.9 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/winapi/^0.3.9

# winapi-rs

Official communication channel: #windows-dev on the [Rust Community Discord](https://discord.gg/aVESxV8)

This crate provides raw FFI bindings to all of Windows API. They are gathered by hand using the Windows 10 SDK from Microsoft. I aim to replace all existing Windows FFI in other crates with this crate through the "[Embrace, extend, and extinguish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embrace,_extend,_and_extinguish)" technique.

If this crate is missing something you need, feel free to create an issue, open a pull request, or contact me via [other means](https://www.rustaceans.org/retep998).

This crate depends on Rust 1.6 or newer on Windows. On other platforms this crate is a no-op and should compile with Rust 1.2 or newer.

## Frequently asked questions

### How do I create an instance of a union?

Use `std::mem::zeroed()` to create an instance of the union, and then assign the value you want using one of the variant methods.

### Why am I getting errors about unresolved imports?

Each module is gated on a feature flag, so you must enable the appropriate feature to gain access to those items. For example, if you want to use something from `winapi::um::winuser` you must enable the `winuser` feature.

### How do I know which module an item is defined in?

You can use the search functionality in the [documentation](https://docs.rs/winapi/) to find where items are defined.

### Why is there no documentation on how to use anything?

This crate is nothing more than raw bindings to Windows API. If you wish to know how to use the various functionality in Windows API, you can look up the various items on [MSDN](https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/windows/desktop/aa906039) which is full of detailed documentation.

### Can I use this library in `no_std` projects?

Yes, absolutely! By default the `std` feature of `winapi` is disabled, allowing you to write Windows applications using nothing but `core` and `winapi`.

### Why is `winapi`'s `HANDLE` incompatible with `std`'s `HANDLE`?

Because `winapi` does not depend on `std` by default, it has to define `c_void` itself instead of using `std::os::raw::c_void`. However, if you enable the `std` feature of `winapi` then it will re-export `c_void` from `std` and cause `winapi`'s `HANDLE` to be the same type as `std`'s `HANDLE`.

### Should I still use those `-sys` crates such as `kernel32-sys`?

No. Those crates are a legacy of how `winapi` 0.2 was organized. Starting with `winapi` 0.3 all definitions are directly in `winapi` itself, and so there is no longer any need to use those `-sys` crates.

## Example

Cargo.toml:

```
[]
 = {  = "0.3",  = ["winuser"] }
```
main.rs:

```
 extern crate winapi;
use Error;
```
## Financial Support

Do you use `winapi` in your projects? If so, you may be interested in financially supporting me on [Patreon](https://www.patreon.com/retep998). Companies in particular are especially encouraged to donate (I'm looking at you [Microsoft](https://github.com/Azure/iotedge/tree/master/edgelet)).

# file-guard 0.2.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/file-guard/latest/source/README.md

```
![Verify](https://github.com/kalamay/file-guard/workflows/Verify/badge.svg?branch=main)
A cross-platform library for simple advisory file locking in Rust.
Take a look at the [Documentation](https://docs.rs/file-guard/) for details!
The lock supports both exclusive and shared locking modes for a byte range
of an opened `File` object. Exclusively locking a portion of a file denies
all other processes both shared and exclusive access to the specified
region of the file. Shared locking a portion of a file denies all processes
exclusive access to the specified region of the file. The locked range does
not need to exist within the file, and the ranges may be used for any
arbitrary advisory locking protocol between processes.
The result of a [`lock()`], [`try_lock()`], or [`lock_any()`] is a
[`FileGuard`]. When dropped, this [`FileGuard`] will unlock the region of
the file currently held. Exclusive locks may be [`.downgrade()`]'ed to
either a shared lock cross platform.
On Unix systems `fcntl` is used to perform the locking, and on Windows, `LockFileEx`.
All generally available behavior is consistent across platforms. For platform-
specific behavior, traits may be used for the respective platform. For example,
on Windows, locks cannot be safely upgraded, whereas on Unix systems, this can
be done safely and atomically. To use this feature, the
[`file_guard::os::unix::FileGuardExt`] may `use`ed, enabling the [`.upgrade()`]
and [`.try_upgrade()`] methods.
Note that on Windows, the file must be open with write permissions to lock it.
```rust
use file_guard::Lock;
use std::fs::OpenOptions;
let mut file = OpenOptions::new()
let mut lock = file_guard::lock(&mut file, Lock::Exclusive, 0, 1)?;
write_to_file(&mut lock)?;
// the lock will be unlocked when it goes out of scope
```
You can store one or more locks in a struct:
```rust
use file_guard::{FileGuard, Lock};
use std::fs::{File, OpenOptions};
let file = OpenOptions::new()
struct Thing<'file> {
}
let t = Thing {
};
// both locks will be unlocked when t goes out of scope
```
Anything that can `Deref` or `DerefMut` to a `File` can be used with the [`FileGuard`].
This works with `Rc<File>`:
```rust
use file_guard::{FileGuard, Lock};
use std::fs::{File, OpenOptions};
use std::rc::Rc;
let file = Rc::new(
);
struct Thing {
}
let t = Thing {
};
// both locks will be unlocked and the file will be closed when t goes out of scope
```
```

# vmap 0.6.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/vmap/0.6.3

# vmap-rs

A cross-platform library for fast and safe memory-mapped IO and boundary-free ring buffer.

This library defines a convenient API for reading and writing to files
using the hosts virtual memory system, as well as allocating memory and
creating circular memory regions. The design of the API strives to
both minimize the frequency of mapping system calls while still retaining
safe access. Critically, it never attempts the own the `File` object used
for mapping. That is, it never clones it or in any way retains it. While
this has some implications for the API (i.e. [ .flush()](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.MapMut.html#method.flush)), it cannot cause
bugs outside of this library through

`File`'s leaky abstraction when cloned
and then closed.The [ Map](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.Map.html) and

[types are primary means for allocating virtual memory regions, both for a file and anonymously. Generally, the](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.MapMut.html)

`MapMut`[and](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.Map.html#method.with_options)

`Map::with_options()`[are used to specify the mapping requirements. See](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.MapMut.html#method.with_options)

`MapMut::with_options()`[for more information.](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.Options.html)

`Options`The [ MapMut](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.MapMut.html) type maintains interior mutability for the mapped memory,
while the

[is read-only. However, it is possible to convert between these types (](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.Map.html)

`Map`[and](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.Map.html#method.into_map_mut)

`.into_map_mut()`[) assuming the proper](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.MapMut.html#method.into_map)

`.into_map()`[are specified.](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.Options.html)

`Options`Additionally, a variety of buffer implementations are provided in the
[ vmap::io](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/io/index.html) module. The

[and](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/io/struct.Ring.html)

`Ring`[use cross-platform optimzed circular memory mapping to remove the typical boundary problem with most circular buffers. This ensures all ranges of the underlying byte buffer can be viewed as a single byte slice, event when the value wraps back around to the beginning of the buffer. The](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/io/struct.InfiniteRing.html)

`InfiniteRing`[and](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/io/struct.BufReader.html)

`BufReader`[implement buffered I/O using a](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/io/struct.BufWriter.html)

`BufWriter`[as a backing layer.](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/io/struct.Ring.html)

`Ring`Take a look at the [Documentation](https://docs.rs/vmap/) for details!

# Examples

```
use Map;
use ;
let path = "example";
// Write some test data
write?;
// Map the first 4 bytes
let  = with_options.len.open?;
assert_eq!;
// Reuse the file to map a different region
let map = with_options.offset.len.map?;
assert_eq!;
```
If opened properly, the [ Map](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.Map.html) can be moved into a

[and modifications to the underlying file can be performed:](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/struct.MapMut.html)

`MapMut````
use Map;
use ;
let path = "example";
// Write some test data
write?;
// Open with write permissions so the Map can be converted into a MapMut
let  = with_options.write.len.open?;
assert_eq!;
// Move the Map into a MapMut
// ... we could have started with MapMut::with_options()
let mut map = map.into_map_mut?;
map.clone_from_slice;
// Flush the changes to disk synchronously
map.flush?;
// Move the MapMut back into a Map
let map = map.into_map?;
assert_eq!;
```
## Ring Buffer

The [ vmap](https://docs.rs/vmap/) library contains a

[that constructs a circular memory allocation where values can wrap from around from the end of the buffer back to the beginning with sequential memory addresses. The](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/io/struct.Ring.html)

`Ring`[is similar, however it allows writes to overwrite reads.](https://docs.rs/vmap/0.6.3/vmap/io/struct.InfiniteRing.html)

`InfiniteRing````
use ;
use ;
let mut buf = new.unwrap;
let mut i = 1;
// Fill up the buffer with lines.
while buf.write_len > 20
// No more space is available.
assert!;
let mut line = Stringnew;
// Read the first line written.
let len = buf.read_line?;
assert_eq!;
line.clear;
// Read the second line written.
let len = buf.read_line?;
assert_eq!;
// Now there is enough space to write more.
write!?;
```

# system_error - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/system_error/^0.2/

## Expand description

A library for cross platform system errors.

This library captures the behavior and messaging for `errno` on unix platforms,
`GetLastError()` on Windows, and `kern_return_t` on macOS and iOS. Additionally,
these [ Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html) values can be converted into

`std::io::Error` values.[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

On Linux:

```
use system_error::Error;
use std::io::ErrorKind;
let os_error = Error::from_raw_os_error(1);
assert_eq!(os_error.kind(), ErrorKind::PermissionDenied);
assert_eq!(
    format!("{}", os_error),
    "Operation not permitted (os error 1)"
);
assert_eq!(
    format!("{:?}", os_error),
    "Error { kind: PermissionDenied, message: \"Operation not permitted (os error 1)\" }"
);
let kern_error = Error::from_raw_kernel_error(8);
assert_eq!(kern_error.kind(), ErrorKind::Other);
assert_eq!(
    format!("{}", kern_error),
    "Unknown error (kernel error 8)"
);
assert_eq!(
    format!("{:?}", kern_error),
    "Error { kind: Other, message: \"Unknown error (kernel error 8)\" }"
);
```
On macOS:

```
use system_error::Error;
use std::io::ErrorKind;
let os_error = Error::from_raw_os_error(1);
assert_eq!(os_error.kind(), ErrorKind::PermissionDenied);
assert_eq!(
    format!("{}", os_error),
    "Operation not permitted (os error 1)"
);
assert_eq!(
    format!("{:?}", os_error),
    "Error { kind: PermissionDenied, message: \"Operation not permitted (os error 1)\" }"
);
let kern_error = Error::from_raw_kernel_error(8);
assert_eq!(kern_error.kind(), ErrorKind::PermissionDenied);
assert_eq!(
    format!("{}", kern_error),
    "(os/kern) no access (kernel error 8)"
);
assert_eq!(
    format!("{:?}", kern_error),
    "Error { kind: PermissionDenied, message: \"(os/kern) no access (kernel error 8)\" }"
);
```
On Windows:

```
use system_error::Error;
use std::io::ErrorKind;
let os_error = Error::from_raw_os_error(5);
assert_eq!(os_error.kind(), ErrorKind::PermissionDenied);
assert_eq!(
    format!("{}", os_error),
    "Access is denied. (os error 5)"
);
assert_eq!(
    format!("{:?}", os_error),
    "Error { kind: PermissionDenied, message: \"Access is denied. (os error 5)\" }"
);
let kern_error = Error::from_raw_kernel_error(8);
assert_eq!(kern_error.kind(), ErrorKind::Other);
assert_eq!(
    format!("{}", kern_error),
    "Unknown error (kernel error 8)"
);
assert_eq!(
    format!("{:?}", kern_error),
    "Error { kind: Other, message: \"Unknown error (kernel error 8)\" }"
);
```
